suggestions.rationale: The cited systematic-review evidence specifically concerns nonfunctioning pituitary macroadenomas with documented optic-chiasm compression. A pituitary macroadenoma—or another pituitary neoplasm only when the individual record objectively documents comparable optic-chiasm or optic-pathway compression—can produce clinically important visual-field and visual-acuity impairment through mass effect. This mapping therefore requires documented optic-chiasm/optic-pathway involvement and does not imply that a small pituitary lesion without such compression causes visual impairment.

pathwayIntelligence.causalChain: Pituitary macroadenoma or other objectively documented pituitary neoplasm with optic-chiasm/optic-pathway compression → anatomic mass effect → compatible visual-field and/or visual-acuity impairment.
developmentQuestions: Do MRI or other imaging records document suprasellar extension, optic-chiasm contact/compression, or other optic-pathway involvement by the pituitary neoplasm?
Are formal visual-field testing, visual-acuity testing, or neuro-ophthalmic examinations abnormal in a pattern anatomically compatible with the documented compression?
Did visual impairment begin or worsen after the compressive pituitary lesion was established, and did it change after decompression or other tumor treatment?
Which competing ophthalmologic, neurologic, vascular, medication-related, or age-related causes of visual impairment should be addressed?
Can endocrinology, neurosurgery, ophthalmology, or neuro-ophthalmology relate the documented visual deficit to the individual lesion rather than to an alternative cause?
issuesToResolve: The evidence is strongest for pituitary macroadenomas with documented chiasmal compression and should not be generalized to all pituitary neoplasms.
Imaging anatomy, objective visual testing, chronology, treatment response, and competing visual diagnoses require individual review.

evidenceGaps: Pituitary MRI or other imaging documenting lesion size, suprasellar extension, and optic-chiasm/optic-pathway relationship
Neuro-ophthalmology, ophthalmology, neurosurgery, or endocrinology assessment of the anatomic relationship
Clinical chronology of tumor detection, visual symptoms, and treatment response
Assessment of competing causes of visual-field or visual-acuity impairment

sourceReferences.citation: Pelsma ICMP et al. Quality of care evaluation in non-functioning pituitary adenoma with chiasm compression: visual outcomes and timing of intervention clinical recommendations based on a systematic literature review and cohort study. Pituitary. 2020;23(4):417-429. PMID 32419072
sourceReferences.note: Systematic review of 44 studies involving 4,789 patients with nonfunctioning pituitary macroadenoma/chiasmal compression evaluated visual dysfunction and outcomes after decompression. Supports an anatomy-specific compressive visual pathway, not visual impairment from every pituitary neoplasm.
